Title: The Standard for Thesauri
QuestionDetail: Which international standard covers the construction of thesauri and their interoperability with other vocabularies, superseding the older ISO 2788 and ISO 5964?
AnswerDetails: ISO 25964 is the thesaurus standard, in two parts. Part 1 covers thesauri for information retrieval - term selection, the hierarchical and associative relationships, scope notes, multilingual handling. Part 2 covers mapping and interoperability between a thesaurus and other vocabularies, which is the part you reach for the day you have to reconcile two of them. It replaced ISO 2788 (monolingual) and ISO 5964 (multilingual). Of the others: ISO 9001 is quality management, ISO 27001 is information security, and ISO 15926 is industrial process-plant data - all real standards, none of them about building a vocabulary.

Title: Why skos:broader Is Not Transitive
QuestionDetail: In SKOS, skos:broader is deliberately NOT declared a transitive property, and a separate skos:broaderTransitive exists alongside it. Why split them?
AnswerDetails: If skos:broader were transitive you could never ask 'what is this concept's immediate parent?' - every ancestor up the chain would answer, and the direct link would become unrecoverable. SKOS therefore keeps skos:broader as the direct relationship and provides skos:broaderTransitive, of which skos:broader is a sub-property, for applications that need the whole chain - most often to expand a search query to everything filed underneath a concept. The convention that follows is worth remembering: you assert the direct links only, and let a reasoner infer the transitive closure.
OptionA: Because transitive closure is too expensive to compute
OptionB: So that applications can reliably read a concept's DIRECT parent, with transitive closure available separately when it is wanted
OptionC: Because SKOS hierarchies are always exactly one level deep
OptionD: Because RDF does not permit transitive properties

Title: Forty Orphans
QuestionDetail: An audit of your taxonomy finds 40 concepts with no broader term and no narrower terms, none of which were intended as top concepts. What is the practical consequence?
AnswerDetails: Orphans are not an error a validator has to reject - they are a discoverability failure, which is why they survive audits that only check for structural validity. A concept unreachable by browsing can be found only by someone who already knows its exact label, and that population is precisely the one that did not need the vocabulary in the first place. Orphans accumulate quietly, usually from bulk imports and from deleting a parent without re-homing its children. A scheduled orphan report is among the cheapest high-value checks a vocabulary team can automate.
OptionA: They are effectively invisible - nobody browsing the hierarchy will reach them, and they surface only on an exact-word search
OptionC: They are duplicated into every branch
OptionD: The concepts are deleted automatically at the next publish

Title: Retiring a Term That Is Already in Use
QuestionDetail: A term must be retired because the business no longer uses it - but thousands of existing records are tagged with it. What is the sound way to handle that?
AnswerDetails: Identifiers are promises. Deleting one breaks every record, link and report that referenced it. Renaming it in place is worse, because it silently rewrites history: records tagged under the old sense now appear to be about something else, and no audit trail says so. Deprecation keeps the identifier resolvable, stops new use, and points at the successor concept so systems and people can migrate deliberately and on their own schedule. This is also the argument for opaque identifiers with labels attached, rather than using the human-readable label itself as the key.
OptionA: Leave it exactly as it is and add the new term alongside it
OptionB: Delete the term and let the affected records fall back to untagged
OptionC: Deprecate it - keep the identifier, mark it as closed to new use, and record a replacement relationship to its successor
OptionD: Rename the term in place to the new name

Title: Two Indexers, One Set of Documents
QuestionDetail: You give the same 50 documents to two trained indexers using the same taxonomy and compare their tagging. What are you measuring, and what does a low score usually mean?
AnswerDetails: Inter-indexer consistency is the honest test of whether a vocabulary is usable by anyone other than its author, and a low score is almost always a design signal rather than a training one. When two careful people disagree, it is normally because two concepts overlap, or because a scope note does not say where one stops and the next begins. So the repair belongs in the vocabulary - sharpen the scope notes, merge the concepts that turn out to be duplicates, add the sibling term that was missing - and it is very much cheaper than the alternative, which is training people to guess the same way.
OptionA: Inter-indexer consistency; the usual cause is overlapping concepts and vague scope notes, not careless people
OptionB: Compression ratio; the vocabulary has grown too large
OptionC: Query recall; more synonyms need to be added
OptionD: Search latency; the index needs rebuilding
